newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan rights group assails government's record.
newsitem.headline: Jordan rights group assails government's record.

text.p: Jordan's main human rights group accused Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti's government on Sunday of resorting to widespread torture and intimidation to push through unpopular policies.

The Arab Organisation for Human Rights in Jordan said that during the eight months since Kabariti's government was sworn in, authorities had curbed freedom of expression, abused legislation, made arbitrary arrests and tortured detainees.

"The present government has registered the poorest government human rights record since 1989," it said in a report, referring to the year when King Hussein instigated a widespread democratisation process in Jordan.
A government official dismissed the report's findings as baseless and called on the group to offer proof of its charges.
The report cited widespread arrests and testimony from detainees tortured by authorities after last August's unrest in Jordan, which was prompted by cuts in bread subsidies.
Four men who said they were arrested spoke at a news conference held in Amman to present the report.
Kamal Issa Gamu said he was detained for 56 days for taking part in what he said was a peaceful demonstration in the city of Salt calling for bread subsidies to be reinstated.
He said he was beaten in the back with electricity cables and rifle butts while his head was covered.

"All these people were detained, and physically tortured," Labib Qamhawi, vice president of the rights group, told the conference. "Some were beaten, others were forced to stand for days without sleep."
The government detained over 500 people during and after August's civil unrest but has said it released most of them.

Qamhawi said the government was facing growing opposition over a 1994 peace treaty with Israel, Jordan's 180 degree turn from its neighbour Iraq, and tough economic measures aimed at reviving the private sector.
"Instead of accommodating this the government reacted by curbing free expression and...curbing freedoms, until the economic measures which led to rioting in the south," he said.
"Torture has become standard policy in interrogating detainees and this is a dangerous development," he said.
Officials said the torture allegations were untrue.

"The goverment totally denies any torture. That is not the way the government works," Kabariti's press adviser Ghadeer Taher told Reuters. "We have utmost respect for human rights and freedom of expression and I challenge them to prove their baseless allegations."

Qamhawi said the group based its reports on sworn testimony from detainees. Asked if it would provide medical reports or pictures of torture wounds, Qamhawi said the group's priority was to compile and report the complaints it received.
"I myself saw toenails ripped out and moustaches plucked with pliers," he said of a visit he said he made to Suwaqa prison south of Amman in early September.
